group.passage: For almost all of human history, most people lived in the countryside. Even in 1960, only about a third of the world’s population lived in towns and cities. Since then, the balance has shifted steadily. Around 2007, according to World Bank figures, city dwellers came to outnumber country people for the first time: about 3.40 billion against 3.34 billion. This did not happen everywhere at once, however. The chart shows the world average and three very different regions. Europe and Central Asia was already more than half urban in 1960, so its line starts high but rises slowly, especially after 1990. East Asia and the Pacific tells another story. Its share barely moved during the 1960s, then climbed faster than in any other region shown, passing the halfway mark in 2008. Sub-Saharan Africa started from the lowest point. Its share nearly tripled over the next sixty years, yet in 2024 the region still had about 720 million people in the countryside and some 570 million in cities. Such numbers should be read with some care. A United Nations report published in 2007 had expected the turning point a year later, in 2008, so even the date of such a milestone can differ from one set of figures to another. Each country’s statistics office decides for itself what counts as an urban area, and the United Nations then collects and smooths the figures. Even so, the overall direction is clear. The number of people living in urban areas worldwide grew from about 1.03 billion in 1960 to about 4.69 billion in 2024. The United Nations expects the urban share to reach 68 percent by 2050, with close to 90 percent of the growth taking place in Asia and Africa. In 2018 there were 33 cities with more than 10 million people each. Yet such giants are not typical: close to half of the world’s urban population lives in places with fewer than 500,000 people. Making sure that these towns and cities offer safe homes that people can afford is one of the targets of the United Nations’ eleventh Sustainable Development Goal.

translation_zh.text:
城鄉人口的消長

在人類歷史的絕大部分時間裡，大多數人都住在鄉村。即使到了 1960 年，全世界也只有大約三分之一的人口住在城鎮和城市。從那時起，這個平衡就穩定地轉移。根據世界銀行的數字，2007 年前後，住在城市的人第一次多於住在鄉村的人：大約 34.0 億對 33.4 億。不過，這件事並不是在各地同時發生的。

圖表呈現了世界平均和三個非常不同的地區。歐洲與中亞在 1960 年就已經有一半以上的人口住在都市，所以它的線起點很高，但上升得很慢，1990 年以後尤其如此。東亞與太平洋則是另一番景象：它的比例在 1960 年代幾乎沒有變動，之後卻比圖中其他任何地區都上升得快，並在 2008 年超過一半。撒哈拉以南非洲的起點最低。接下來的六十年裡，它的比例增加到將近三倍，但到了 2024 年，這個地區仍有大約 7.2 億人住在鄉村，城市裡則約有 5.7 億人。

這些數字應該小心解讀。聯合國一份 2007 年發表的報告原本預估這個轉折點會晚一年，在 2008 年出現，所以連這樣一個里程碑的日期，都可能因不同的數據而有出入。每個國家的統計機關都自己決定什麼地方算是都市地區，再由聯合國蒐集這些數字並加以平滑處理。

即使如此，整體的方向是清楚的。全世界住在都市地區的人數，從 1960 年的大約 10.3 億增加到 2024 年的大約 46.9 億。聯合國預估到 2050 年，都市人口的比例會達到 68%，而且將近 90% 的成長會發生在亞洲和非洲。2018 年，全世界有 33 座人口超過一千萬的城市。不過這樣的巨型城市並不是常態：全世界的都市人口中，將近一半住在人口不到 50 萬的地方。確保這些城鎮與城市能提供安全、人們負擔得起的住宅，是聯合國第十一項永續發展目標的目標之一。

【圖 1】住在都市地區的人口比例：世界與三個地區，1960–2020（%）。World：34.2、36.4、39.5、42.8、46.8、51.8、56.4；East Asia & Pacific：24.9、24.9、27.6、33.2、41.6、52、62.4；Sub-Saharan Africa：14.3、18.5、23.4、28.4、32.7、37.5、42.2；Europe & Central Asia：55、60.6、64.9、67.4、68.7、70.6、73.5。
